candidates.label: Pool of Siloam
candidates.support: Wikidata's coordinate matches OpenBible.info's independently recorded point exactly, and corresponds to the monumental stepped pool excavated at the foot of the City of David.

summary.text: The Pool of Siloam is a reservoir at the southern end of Jerusalem's City of David, fed by the Gihon Spring, where the Gospel of John records Jesus sending a man born blind to wash and receive his sight.

history.text: Archaeologists Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron identified a monumental stepped pool from the Second Temple period at the base of the City of David in 2004, which they identify with the Pool of Siloam known to first-century Jerusalem.

scripture.textWEB: Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them—do you think that they were worse offenders than all the men who dwell in Jerusalem?
and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So he went away, washed, and came back seeing.
He answered, “A man called Jesus made mud, anointed my eyes, and said to me, ‘Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.’ So I went away and washed, and I received sight.”

otConnections.note: Nehemiah's account of rebuilding Jerusalem's walls mentions the 'pool of Shelah' (Siloam) by the king's garden, an earlier water installation on the same site later associated with the Second Temple-period pool of John 9.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch."

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Quirinius, governing Syria, conducted a census at the start of this period. Luke 2:1-2 is dated by some instead to the time of Herod's birth narrative, before 4 BC, rather than to Quirinius's AD 6 census; this note does not resolve the question.

Roman province of Judea (ruler: Legates, with a legion now based at Jerusalem)
politicalHistory.note: An administrative upgrade (a praetorian legate instead of a procurator), not a border or name change.
